claims.text: At stage-2 OrderService.CancelOrderAsync calls order.Cancel(), then notifier.Send(order, "order cancelled"), then repository.SaveChangesAsync(); ShipOrderAsync does the same with order.Ship() and "order shipped".
At stage-2 notifier.Send (QueuedNotifier) adds a pending row to notifications, the email job of backend.l2.database-job-queue, saved by the same SaveChangesAsync.

At stage-3 Order has `private readonly List<IDomainEvent> domainEvents` exposed as `IReadOnlyList<IDomainEvent> DomainEvents => domainEvents.AsReadOnly()`, plus ClearDomainEvents() (also called by the dispatcher); Order holds no subscriber, notifier or handler reference.

Order.Cancel() at stage-3 throws OrderStatusException when Status is cancelled, shipped, paid or refunding; only after `Status = "cancelled"` does it add `new OrderCancelled(this, DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)`; it calls no other object.

DomainEvents.cs at stage-3: IDomainEvent declares only `Order Order` and `DateTimeOffset OccurredAt`; OrderPlaced, OrderCancelled, OrderShipped (and three refund records) are sealed positional records implementing it with exactly those two values.

Order's constructor records OrderPlaced before the order has an id (its primary key); EfOrderRepository.AddAsync assigns it afterwards from the orders sequence, before handlers run (DomainEvents.cs comment).

OrderTests at stage-3: both tests call order.ClearDomainEvents() before Cancel() to drop setup events; Cancel_NewOrder_RecordsOrderCancelled asserts one OrderCancelled in DomainEvents; Cancel_ShippedOrder_RecordsNothing asserts it empty after the throwing Cancel; neither uses a fake.

A raised C# event (multicast delegate) calls each subscriber synchronously, in subscription order, inside the raising method; an uncaught subscriber exception reaches the raising method and later subscribers are not called; an instance-method delegate references its instance.
claims.source_hint: C# docs: Events (Handling and raising events); Using Delegates (multicast invocation order, exceptions, instance reference)

claims.text: samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Design/OrderEvents.cs (stage-2 and stage-3), a sample class separate from Order, declares `public event Action<int>? OrderPlaced` and Place raises it with `OrderPlaced?.Invoke(orderId)`.

Naming a domain event in the past tense after what happened (OrderCancelled), not after one reaction (SendCancellationEmail), keeps it true when more reactions are added; this is tactical DDD naming guidance, not a C# rule.

A domain event holding an in-process Order object is not itself sent between programs; data for another program is a separate DTO holding values such as the order id (OrderMessage, backend/messaging), made in a separate step. Opposing usage: some teams call those 'events' too.

`git grep -n "domainEvents.Add" stage-3 -- DonHang.Domain` in examples/don-hang prints six lines, all DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs (87, 132, 142, 155, 165, 176); `git grep -n "Status = " stage-3 -- DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs` also lists MarkPaid (109-114), which adds no event.

claims.text: At stage-3 OrderService.CancelOrderAsync calls order.Cancel(), then events.DispatchAsync(order), then repository.SaveChangesAsync(); no notifier.Send. Reactions are written once in classes outside OrderService (NotifyCustomerOnOrderEvents, RecordOrderStatusHistory).

If a C# event subscriber sent the email at once inside Cancel() and the later save failed, the customer would be told of a cancellation that was never stored; reasoning from claim 8, not a library behaviour.
